# Can PM ever be “just a job”? (SF Bay Area)

## Post details
r/ProductManagement | 234 upvotes | 112 comments | Posted by u/cheesy_luigi on 2026-02-27T02:28:19.959Z

## Content
I’m a PM in San Francisco and have gotten increasingly burnt out over the past few years. While there are many aspects of product that I enjoy, including the joy I get from some coworkers and customers and being able to creatively solve problems, it can be overshadowed by workaholic coworkers, company leaders force feeding AI and pushing unrealistic launches, and working in an uninteresting product space. I realize that I’m paid to care, but it’s getting harder and harder to fake it, especially being in a space where so many other PMs boast of long hours and intensity. Bay Area PMs, have you had success making PM “just a job?

## Top Comments
- Well long hours doesn’t translate to good PM.. this job is more about delivering value to users and business. I have seen that many companies and PMs just focus on delivering tickets or features, but lack the strategic thinking. That’s failed PM.
- I think you also have to figure out WHY you became a Product Manager in the first place: - Was it to work hard to deliver an impact to users across the globe. - Was it just for the paycheck? - Was it to eventually move into a startup or do your own thing? I do think burnout is real, but we need to also stay grounded into what we value in our day-to-day still, and WHY we're doing this job.
- Very hard if you’re in a company that is trying to figure out things. Public listed companies or stable companies are good. but again if you want to be in the forefront of technology and breakthrough, these old companies may not be the best choice
- Do you think better coordination inside the teams and better inter-connexions between the tools could drastically help PMs to be more productive and spend less time and low importance tasks ?
- For me, as a new parent, I've realized it's understanding what you control. Alot of things are outside of your control, but take ownership, attempt to influence, but also step back and realize it's not controllable. Ultimately, I start to get less emotionally attached to the work, and that has been freeing for me. Also just setting boundaries and sticking to them helps. Most things you obsess over, won't actually impact your performance or career progression.
- I know that this thread is a year old. Look as I used to work as a Product Manager and have coached many of them and this is super common. My take: burnout is way too common. I have horror stories from several clients about mental and physical health issues, complete breakdowns and what not. Here is my honest opinion though - the burnout is not about hours. I probably work more now than I used to as a Product Manager but I never feel burned out. I LOVE what I do. But its hard to care all the time. It can seem like faking it when you work on a product that you don't care about and have to worry about appearing good than actually doing good work. A few things I'd think about: You don't need to match other people's intensity to be successful. This is HARD. But I have seen people who set amazing boundaries and protect their time. They never seemed to do anything after 5 PM. It's a small minority, but it's possible. Get a coach. Not me as I don't coach in this area but maybe a mindset coach or just a high performance coach. The investment is probably worth it.
- I feel this post so much. I joined a Big Tech company and we have such a bad culture. Everything is on fire, everything is due yesterday, meetings pop up on calendar anytime, they get cancelled five mins in when we are waiting for folks to show up, there's no documentation. I am expected to work at great velocity without any support. I am expected to work early morning with folks in EU and sometimes late night in Asia. And of course I am not paid that much and can get laid off anytime. This company is rated 4+ on Glassdoor. I sure hope that my company and/or manager are an exception and that there are better teams out there. I have a family and cant be always on. I dont know if this is a Bay Area thing and east coast would be better, or the country itself is like this.
- At some point you realize it’s better to just be a founder.
- Ya, you have to set boundaries or the job will eat you alive. Unlike some other roles, PMs are never "done." Always more to do. So, you have to set boundaries. When my child was born, I decided that I was going to leave the office at 5pm. Full stop. I would go home and have dinner with my wife and daughter. I was able to make that stick for eighteen years until she became an adult. Yes, sometimes I didn't make it home in time, but most of the time I did. I would sometimes work after she went to bed or get up extra early, but most of the time I was home. And since this was the only time all of us were together on most work days, it was a precious time for me. During that time I did quite well and eventually got promoted to Senior Director of PM. I've worked in SV for over 30 years. Of the six bosses I had during that time, only one refused to honor my family time. I wound up quitting that job for that reason.
- Plenty of companies care at least a little about the work/life balance of their employees, if only because they understand that a better balance results in better quality output. You tend to want to find mid to large sized companies that aren't like, FAANG level. I find that small companies still expect a lot out of you.
